A simple copper-alloy sealing ring found at Herodium in Gideon Foerster's 1968–69 dig, and published in 2018, has a krater (wine bowl) engraved on it with tiny Greek letters read as 'of Pilatus'. The publishing team said it was unlikely to be Pontius Pilate's own ring, but raised the possibility that it belonged to someone in his administration or to another man named Pilatus.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable find: the ring, its findspot (Herodium, in a layer buried before the fortress fell in 71 CE) and the reading Πιλάτο(υ) are reported in the 2018 IEJ article (JSTOR 26740648). Eck & Ecker's 2024 abstract, which was read, confirms the 1968/69 Foerster find, the 2018 publication and the reading 'of Pilate', and says the published interpretations all linked the ring 'directly or indirectly' to Pilate. What weakens this side: the 2018 authors themselves call a link to Pontius Pilate only a possibility. Pilatus was a family name used by others, the letters are small and partly deformed, and the ring's krater is a Jewish motif made locally. The IEJ article was not opened directly (JSTOR access challenge).

claims.text: Werner Eck and Avner Ecker (ʿAtiqot 2024) argue the ring is not connected to Pontius Pilate. They say the reading itself is problematic. A Roman official's ring would use Latin, the language of Roman administration in the early 1st century, not Greek. And the ring more probably belonged to a local Jew. They also discuss other ways to read the letters.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable source: the ʿAtiqot 110 abstract (doi.org/10.70967/2948-040X.1083, read) states that 'apart from the problematic reading', everything known about Roman provincial administration, especially the use of Greek in an administrative context in the first half of the 1st century, speaks against linking the ring to Pilate, and that alternative readings are discussed. What weakens this side: it is an argument from Roman practice and epigraphy, not a new find; it does not prove whose ring it was. The full PDF could not be fetched (403), so only the abstract was read.

Place-name continuity: the ruins called Khirbet Karazeh (Korazim) keep a form of the name Chorazin, one of the towns Jesus denounced (Matthew 11:21; Luke 10:13). Eusebius (early 4th century) describes Chorazin as a deserted village two miles from Capernaum, which fits the location of these ruins.
claims.strength_reason: Checkable basis: BiblePlaces lists Kh. Karraza / Karazeh / Kerazeh / Korazim among the site's names. Eusebius' Onomasticon, entry 976 (Wolf 1971 translation on tertullian.org, read 2026-10-27), places Chorazin, the Galilee town Jesus reproached in the Gospel, as a deserted village two miles from Capernaum. The app's own pins put the ruins about 3.6 km from Capernaum in a straight line (2 Roman miles is about 3 km). Two independent lines, the surviving name and a 4th-century location, point to the same ruins, which is why it is rated strong. What weakens it: no inscription naming the town was read, and the visible synagogue is late Roman (BiblePlaces dates it to the 2nd century AD), not from Jesus' time. BiblePlaces also notes an unpublished 1926 report by J. Ory of an earlier building about 200 m west, which was not verified.

claims.text: Visible synagogue is later than Jesus; earlier settlement evidence exists but the famous carved synagogue is post-NT.
claims.strength_reason: The visible synagogue is a 'Galilean'-style basalt building (BiblePlaces, Chorazin), a type generally dated after the New Testament period, so it is not the synagogue of Jesus' day.

recent_updates.title: Ophel purification complex: layout and 280 m² area confirmed
recent_updates.text: The Hebrew University release describes a pool about 12 × 9.5 m with steps on all four sides; northwest of it, an ashlar building of four rooms, three of them public ritual baths (mikva’ot); a paved forecourt between them; and large drains toward the Kidron. Altogether the complex covers about 280 m² (about 3,000 sq ft). One mikveh survives to its full 4.2 m height with its vault. Built in the early 1st century CE over an earlier 1st-century-BCE ashlar bath complex, it ended in 70 CE (First Revolt coins on its floors).
recent_updates.solidity: High (university excavation); use by pilgrims is the excavators’ interpretation
recent_updates.caveat: The nearby total of 18 pools over about 1,600 m² is the Armstrong Institute’s count across older digs, not this complex.

claims.text: Mazar Temple Mount Excavations / Ophel & SW corner (NT-period streets)
Herodian street under Robinson’s Arch; fallen ashlars from 70 CE destruction; Ophel walls; ritual baths; monumental stair approaches to Temple Mount.

These show the scale of the Temple approaches in Jesus' day. The walls still standing is a reminder that Jesus' 'not one stone' words (Mark 13:2) were about the Temple buildings, not the retaining walls.
claims.strength_reason: The walls, the Master Course stone (about 13 m, 517 t) and the remains of Robinson's Arch are visible and measured (BiblePlaces, Western Wall); the IAA report on Robinson's Arch describes the Herodian paved street and drainage channel beside the wall. What weakens it: this is architecture that shows the setting, not proof of any Gospel event.

claims.text: Robinson's Arch fell after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, according to the IAA excavators. Fallen Herodian stones still lie on the street below the wall. This fits Jesus' words that the Temple buildings would be thrown down (Mark 13:2), but dating each fallen stone is debated.
claims.strength_reason: The IAA's 2011 Robinson's Arch report (Shukron & Reich) states that the arch collapsed after the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, and it shows that two fallen voussoirs in the drainage channel are NOT from that collapse (they fell during building). What weakens it: the report says this only in passing and does not publish the dating evidence for the stone pile; Shimon Gibson (2014) has argued that a large stone collapse north of the arch came from the 363 CE earthquake, not from 70 CE.
